results.title: Distributed-systems consistency patterns | by Alice Dai | Medium
results.content: # Distributed-systems consistency patterns. Here’s a practical **taxonomy of distributed-systems consistency patterns** — grouped so you can pick the right tool fast. (Think: how we *coordinate*, *replicate*, *order*, *transact*, and *heal* data.). ## 1) Consistency models & session guarantees (what reads are allowed). * **Strong / Linearizability / External consistency** (e.g., Spanner TrueTime): reads reflect the latest committed write. * **Snapshot Isolation / Repeatable Read / Read Committed** (MVCC flavors). * **Session guarantees:** Read-your-writes, Monotonic reads/writes, Writes-follow-reads. * **Eventual consistency / Bounded staleness / Prefix consistency** (common in geo or AP systems). ## 2) Write coordination & consensus (who’s allowed to write, and when). * **Distributed locks & leases:** ZooKeeper/etcd/Consul, **fencing tokens**, Redlock (controversial). ## 3) Distributed transactions & workflows (spanning boundaries). * **Transactional Outbox** (+ **Inbox**) a.k.a. transactional messaging. * **Change Data Capture (CDC)** (e.g., Debezium) from WAL to streams. ## 5) Conflict detection & resolution (when writes collide). * **Version vectors / Vector clocks** (detect concurrent updates). * **Last-Write-Wins (LWW)** / custom merge policies. * **Kafka transactions** (EOS) for consume-transform-produce chains (broker-side atomicity). * **Outbox/Inbox** pair for DB↔broker **dual-write** safety. ## 7) Read-side & cache consistency (serving fast without lying). * **Cache-aside (lazy)**, **Read-through**, **Write-through**, **Write-back**. * **CQRS** & **materialized views** (async read models), **event-carried state transfer**. * **Session stickiness** for read-after-write guarantees. * **Optimistic concurrency (OCC/CAS)**: version columns, ETags, conditional updates. * **MVCC** (multi-version concurrency control). ## 9) Ordering & snapshots (seeing a consistent cut). ## 10) Data distribution choices (consistency implications). * **Sharding/partitioning** (hash/range), **consistent hashing** (vnodes). * **Client-side routing vs coordinator**, **sticky vs any-node** reads/writes. * **“No lost events across DB → Kafka”** → **Transactional Outbox + Inbox**, idempotent consumers. * **“Cross-service order workflow with refunds”** → **Saga** (orchestrator) or **TCC**. * **“Prevent overselling inventory/slots”** → **CAS/conditional updates** or **atomic Lua (Redis)**; optionally **TCC**. * **“Geo-distributed writes with merges”** → **CRDTs** or **vector-clock + custom merge**; **active-active**. * **“Exactly-once stream processing”** → **Kafka EOS** + idempotent sinks (still use outbox for DB dual-write). * **“Strong consistency on a small cluster”** → **Raft/Paxos** (single-leader), **serializable** transactions. * **“Fast reads from cache but correct on updates”** → **Cache-aside** + **CDC invalidation** + versioned keys.

results.title: Concurrency Control in Distributed Transactions - GeeksforGeeks
results.content: # Concurrency Control in Distributed Transactions. Concurrency control ensures that multiple transactions running concurrently across different sites do not lead to data inconsistency or conflicts. These sub-transactions across every node must be executed serially to maintain data integrity & the concurrency control mechanisms do this serial execution. Pessimistic Concurrency Control (PCC) is a technique used in database systems to prevent conflicts between concurrent transactions by locking data before it is accessed. Without proper isolation, one transaction may read or modify data while another is still processing it, leading to conflicts. The two-phase locking protocol is a concurrency technique used to manage locks on data items in database. > *****Growing Phase*****: The transaction acquires all the locks on the data items that'll be required to execute the transaction successfully. It helps in synchronizing the transaction and their operation so that data integrity is maintained. The Optimistic Concurrency control techniques proceeds on the basis of assumption that, 0 or very few transactions will try to access a certain resource simultaneously. * ****Read Phase****: When a transaction begins, it reads the data while also logging the time-stamp at which data is read to verify for conflicts during the validation phase. * ****Execution Phase****: In this phase, the transaction executes all its operation like create, read, update or delete etc. * ****Validation Phase****: Before committing a transaction, a validation check is performed to ensure consistency by checking the ****last\_updated**** timestamp with the one recorded at read\_phase. ****Example****: Let's say we have two transaction T1 and T2, they operate on data item - A. The Timestamp concurrency technique will keep track of the timestamp when the data was accessed by transaction T1 first time. That way, every transaction can concurrently perform their operations. Transaction ensures that the data item is not changed while it was executing operations on it. CRDTs is a data structure technique which allows a transaction to perform all its operation and replicate the data to some other node or current node. After all the operations are performed, this technique offers us with merging methods that allows us to merge the data across distributed nodes (conflict-free) and eventually achieving consistent state (eventually consistent property). 2 min readMemory Management in Operating System.

results.title: Ensuring Data Consistency Across Distributed Systems: Strategies for Modern Applications | by RapidFork Technology | Medium
results.content: # Ensuring Data Consistency Across Distributed Systems: Strategies for Modern Applications. In this article, we will explore different strategies to ensure data consistency across multiple databases or resources, including Two-Phase Commit (2PC), Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC), and more. **Two-Phase Commit (2PC)** is a protocol that ensures distributed transactions are atomic and consistent across multiple databases or resources. Ensuring data consistency across distributed systems is a critical requirement for many modern applications. The strategies discussed in this article, including 2PC, OCC, and various approaches for handling failures and recovery, can help you achieve data consistency while considering the specific needs and constraints of your application. In conclusion, the challenges of maintaining data consistency across distributed systems are complex, but by using a combination of strategies and technologies, you can successfully navigate these challenges and build enterprise-grade applications. The key is to understand the trade-offs and choose the most suitable strategy for your specific requirements, ensuring that your application remains scalable, resilient, and consistent throughout its lifecycle.
